metadata.description: Disruption what-if: Billerica DC outage and Norwood contingency, re-optimized.

storymap.title: What if Billerica goes down?
storymap.subtitle: Disruption what-if and contingency activation
storymap.footer: Illustrative sample data. Site locations approximate; customers, suppliers, volumes and rates are invented.

chapters.title: Normal operations
chapters.description:
Billerica – Enterprise Rd ships Critical Care and Bioprocess to most North American customers.

Customers within SLA: 97.9% (46/47)
Avg transit: 1.2 days
Weekly freight: $33,665
Weekly CO₂e: 4,265 kg

Sample data: Nova sites from the ERP/CRM footprint (locations approximate); customers, suppliers, volumes and rates are illustrative.

chapters.title: Billerica DC goes offline
chapters.description:
The engine re-plans instantly: Critical Care and Bioprocess demand falls back to the UK hub by international air. 25 customers fall outside SLA.

Customers within SLA: 46.8% (22/47)
Avg transit: 2.8 days
Weekly freight: $131,526 (+291% vs normal)
Weekly CO₂e: 16,475 kg (+286% vs normal)

chapters.title: The impact lands on hospitals
chapters.description: Hospital Critical Care customers have a 2-day SLA; a transatlantic air lane with customs takes 3. Every red ring is a hospital that would wait longer for analyzers and consumables.

chapters.title: Activate Norwood as the contingency DC
chapters.description:
Pre-positioning Critical Care and Bioprocess stock at Norwood restores service at near-normal cost.

Customers within SLA: 97.9% (46/47)
Avg transit: 1.2 days
Weekly freight: $33,857 (+1% vs normal)
Weekly CO₂e: 4,266 kg (+0% vs normal)

This is the quantified case for a contingency stocking policy, the same plan the Continuity Command Center would execute.

chapters.title: Recovered network
chapters.description: Same customers, same SLAs: served from Norwood while Billerica is down.
